description: I am Saummya Salve. My interests include Computer Vision, Artifical Intelligence and Astrophysics.
summary:
The SPHEREx Sky Time-Lapse Explorer is a web-based, free application which takes NASA's SPHEREx infrared images and makes them into a time-lapse of any part of the sky. Just enter your target's name or coordinate, and it will pull down all SPHEREx images for that location from the IRSA archives at NASA. It will then align the images and stack each 6 month passage across the sky. After this process has completed, you may choose to see the final product as a video, cycle through the different times, create a "difference" image, or create a "deep stack."

The instrument is designed to measure the velocity of moving objects and compare the results with the Gaia catalogue from ESA. This device can generate a 0.75-5 µm spectrum of every star that is selected by the user. In addition, the software can create light curves for all variable stars. A single click of the mouse will scan an area for moving objects and identify those not listed in Gaia as potential discoveries.

We used the SPHEREx method to test against target objects. For Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855, the motion we observed agreed with published values. The brown dwarfs, that Gaia rarely, if ever, observes, were measured solely using SPHEREx data. The spectrum of Epsilon Indi B exhibited absorption lines due to water and methane. Additionally, an MCP server provides access to similar tools for AI assistants.

This makes SPHEREx data usable by anyone for finding nearby cold objects.
details:
1. Project Details

What it does
SPHEREx Sky Time-Lapse Explorer is a free web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a time-lapse of any patch of sky. A user picks one of the challenge targets, or types any sky coordinates (RA/Dec), and the tool:

  • queries NASA/IPAC IRSA live for every SPHEREx image covering that spot and downloads small cutouts;
  • re-projects each image onto one fixed, north-up sky grid, so background stars stay still and anything that moves or changes stands out;
  • groups the images into six-month sky passes and stacks each one.

The result can be viewed four ways: a Movie, a Blink between first and last pass (the method used to discover Pluto), a Difference image where movers appear as red/blue pairs, and a Deep stack for faint objects.

Science tools

  • Proper-motion measurement with a saturation-aware PSF fit, compared with ESA Gaia DR3.
  • A 0.75–5 µm spectrum of any star you click, built from SPHEREx’s 102 colours, with water, methane, CO and CO₂ bands marked.
  • Light curves for variable stars.
  • A one-click scan that finds every moving source and flags movers that are missing from Gaia as discovery candidates.
  • Gaia stars drawn on the image, and an RGB view (D6/D3/D1) in which cold brown dwarfs look red.
  • An MCP server that lets AI assistants use the same tools.

Results

  • Barnard’s Star: 10.17 ± 0.44″/yr vs 10.39″/yr from Gaia DR3.
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.53 and 4.51″/yr from two independent detectors vs 4.71″/yr published. It isn’t in Gaia at all.
  • WISE 0855: invisible in single images, but measured at 8.96 ± 1.21″/yr on stacked passes vs 8.13″/yr published.
  • The spectrum of Epsilon Indi B shows water and methane absorption, the signature of a cold brown-dwarf atmosphere.

Benefits and impact
SPHEREx data normally sits in an archive as hundreds of raw files per position. Our tool makes it usable by students and citizen scientists, who can hunt for nearby cold objects that Gaia cannot see, as WiseView volunteers did with WISE.

What we considered

  • Saturated bright stars, which the motion fit works around.
  • Very faint objects, which are measured on stacked images.
  • Archive outages: the tool retries, caches results, and falls back to saved data.
  • Honest uncertainties, and clear labels for anything unverified.

Tools
Python (FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, pyvo), HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Chart.js, and the MCP Python SDK.
